question: Will any of OpenAI’s “Ten Advances in Math and Theoretical CS” be shown to be flawed by the end of August?
resolution_criteria:
[tweet]YES if, by August 31, there is a consensus in credible reporting or within the academic community that at least one of the core arguments or main theorems in OpenAI's "Ten Advances" is fatally flawed or incorrect. Otherwise, resolves NO.

"Flawed" means a core mathematical or theoretical error is identified that invalidates the main result of the paper, and the error is either unfixable or difficult to patch.

Nitpicks—such as minor typos, formatting errors, minor translation gaps in the Lean formalization that do not undermine the mathematical proof's validity, or easily patchable edge cases—do not count toward a YES resolution.
research:
I found no sign, as of Aug 16, of a confirmed error that invalidates any of the ten results. The criticism so far is about credit and novelty, not correctness. Most pages would not load through the proxy, so the dates and details below come from search summaries and are marked as unverified where needed.

## 1. Resolution source
- There is no single data series. The question resolves on whether credible reporting or the academic community agrees that a main result is fatally flawed.
- 2026-08-01: OpenAI published "Ten Advances in Mathematics and Theoretical Computer Science," a 249-page PDF of results from an internal model said to be "Astra." [PDF](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/ten-proofs-oai.pdf), [blog](https://openai.com/index/sharing-ai-progress-in-mathematics/) (blog page would not load)
- The topics include high-dimensional sphere packing, binary and spherical codes, the first construction of a non-sofic group, a disproof of Connes's rigidity conjecture, arithmetic circuit complexity, quantum parallel repetition, and three Erdős problems. [TNW](https://thenextweb.com/news/openai-astra-model-ten-math-proofs-non-sofic-groups), [LessWrong](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/pQYEPitFqztcRvBsS/openai-s-unreleased-model-astra-solves-ten-major-open)
- The Lean 4 proof files are on GitHub. Secondary reports say they contain zero "sorry" placeholders (Lean's marker for an unproven step). [GitHub](https://github.com/openai/ten-proofs), [s5labs](https://s5labs.io/resources/insights/openai-astra-ten-math-proofs-lean-certificates/)
- The resolver is the Manifold market creator, "Sketchy." [Manifold](https://manifold.markets/Sketchy/will-any-of-openais-ten-advances-in)

## 2. Current status
- As of 2026-08-16: I found no withdrawn result, no OpenAI correction of a theorem, and no expert agreement that any main theorem is wrong.
- Lean checks the logic of each proof. The main remaining way to a YES is a wrong formal statement (the Lean theorem not matching the claimed result) or an error in a result that is not fully formalized. I found no report of either.
- 2026-08 (date unclear): an arXiv preprint, "A Human Audit of OpenAI's AI-Generated Mathematical Proofs" (arXiv:2608.14673), reviewed the results. Its number points to mid-to-late August and it would not load, so I can't confirm its date or findings. [arXiv](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.14673)

## 3. Recent news (newest first)
- Mid-August, dates uncertain: the criticism centers on credit and novelty:
  - Steven Miller (Yeshiva University) says the sphere-packing proof reused an argument from a 2016 paper he co-wrote without credit, and calls it possible "research misconduct." This attacks credit, not correctness. [AI Weekly](https://aiweekly.co/alerts/openais-astra-math-proofs-draw-research-misconduct-claims)
  - Reports say OpenAI quietly reworded its claims that nobody had made progress on these problems for decades. [Kingy](https://kingy.ai/news/openai-astra-ten-math-results-evidence/)
- Early to mid-August: independent mathematicians began checking the Lean files line by line. [Startup Fortune](https://startupfortune.com/independent-mathematicians-are-now-lean-checking-openais-proof-claims-line-by-line/)
  - One reviewer reported a sign ("polarity") error in Chapter 6, the quantum parallel repetition result. Coverage dated after Aug 16 should not be used here, so the outcome of that claim isn't covered.
- Early August: Thomas Bloom, who reviewed the work, called it "big news." Others pointed out that none of it has been peer reviewed and that credit is unclear. [Datafloq](https://datafloq.com/openai-solved-ten-open-math-problems-nobody-can-say-who-gets-credit/), [DataCamp](https://www.datacamp.com/blog/open-ai-model-astra-solved-ten-open-math-problems)

## 4. Base rates
- I found no formal base rate.
- Past AI math claims have mostly failed on novelty, not correctness. In October 2025, OpenAI's claims that GPT-5 had solved Erdős problems were walked back because the solutions already existed in the literature; the proofs themselves were not wrong. That is from memory, I did not check it here.
- Results that are fully checked in Lean, with no "sorry," are rarely shown to be fatally wrong within weeks. Problems that do appear are usually a formal statement that doesn't match the claim. Human-written major claims get serious errors found more often (for example the 2023 LK-99 superconductor claim and some claimed P vs NP proofs), but those had no formal checking.
- The window is only about 15 days, and real expert agreement on a fatal flaw usually takes longer to form.

## 5. Other forecasts
- Manifold, this question: 39% YES in a snapshot of unknown date. The market's definition of "flawed" matches the one given here. [Manifold](https://manifold.markets/Sketchy/will-any-of-openais-ten-advances-in)
- Manifold, a related market covering the GitHub repo with a November 30 deadline: about 34% YES (snapshot). [Manifold](https://manifold.markets/Sketchy/will-any-of-openais-massive-release)
- I found nothing on Polymarket or Kalshi.

## 6. Upcoming events before Aug 31
- Final or revised versions of the arXiv human audit (2608.14673), including how the Chapter 6 sign-error claim turns out.
- More independent Lean audits, especially comparing the formal statements with the claims in the paper.
- Expert write-ups and any OpenAI errata or reworded claims on its blog or GitHub.
- Further coverage of the Miller credit dispute. On its own this should not count toward YES, since it concerns attribution rather than correctness.
